titleEn: In Your light we see light
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Bb C | Dm Dm |
intro: Thirteen verses that read like two different poems bolted together, and the bolt is the point: four verses of close portraiture of a wicked man, five verses of the widest imagery anywhere in the book, then a short prayer to keep the first away from the speaker. It is not one of the psalms fixed into the daily order of prayer the way Psalm 145 is, and most people meet it through a single line, verse 10. For a learner the useful stretch is verses 6 to 11, which put the same second person possessive ending on eight different nouns in a row: Your kindness, Your faithfulness, Your righteousness, Your judgments, Your wings, Your house, Your delights, Your light.

stichs.en: For the choirmaster.
Of the servant of the LORD, of David.

verses.summary: The heading gives David a title before it gives his name, servant of the LORD, which is rare in the headings and sets up a psalm about two kinds of allegiance.

stichs.en: Transgression speaks to the wicked man deep inside my heart:
there is no dread of God before his eyes.

verses.summary: The psalm opens with an oracle delivered by the wrong speaker. What follows is a diagnosis rather than an accusation: the fault is located in something the man does not feel.

stichs.en: For it flatters him in his own eyes,
too much to find his guilt and hate it.

verses.summary: Self flattery is offered as the mechanism. He cannot locate his own guilt because locating it would need an eye he has stopped using honestly.

stichs.en: The words of his mouth are wickedness and deceit;
he has given up acting wisely, doing good.

verses.summary: Speech and conduct, both corrupted, and the governing verb is one of ceasing. He did not fail at wisdom, he quit it.

stichs.en: He plots wickedness on his bed,
he takes his stand on a road that is not good,
he does not reject evil.

verses.summary: Night, then the road, then a whole disposition. The plotting is deliberate and well rested, which the psalm treats as worse than the crime of impulse.

stichs.en: LORD, Your kindness is in the heavens,
Your faithfulness reaches the clouds.

verses.summary: The camera pulls back with no transition at all. The vocabulary changes completely, and so does the person being addressed.

stichs.en: Your righteousness is like the mountains of God,
Your judgments are the great deep.
Man and beast You save, LORD.

verses.summary: Two similes of scale, one reaching up and one reaching down, and then the surprise at the end: what all that height and depth protects includes animals.

stichs.en: How precious is Your kindness, God.
The children of man take refuge in the shadow of Your wings.

verses.summary: The scale collapses into a shelter small enough to sit under. Wings are the smallest image in this panel and the only one a person can be inside.

stichs.en: They drink their fill from the richness of Your house,
and You give them to drink from the stream of Your delights.

verses.summary: The guests eat and drink in the house of the one just described in cosmic terms. Hospitality is the form the vastness takes when a person meets it.

stichs.en: For with You is the fountain of life;
in Your light we see light.

verses.summary: The line the psalm turns on. Both halves state a condition rather than a reward: life has a source, and sight has a medium.

stichs.en: Keep drawing out Your kindness to those who know You,
and Your righteousness to the upright of heart.

verses.summary: The verb means to pull something out lengthwise, so what is asked for is duration rather than a new gift. Nothing here requests more than is already being given.

stichs.en: Let not the foot of pride come upon me,
and let not the hand of the wicked drive me away.

verses.summary: The petition names its danger with body parts, a foot and a hand, which drops the poem back into the register of the opening portrait.

stichs.en: There the doers of wickedness have fallen,
thrust down, unable to rise.

verses.summary: The end reports a fall the psalm never narrated. The claim stays deliberately small: they are down and cannot get up, not gone.

pardes.body: Two panels and a prayer. Verses 2 to 5 are a portrait of one man, and everything in them is small and enclosed: his eyes, his mouth, his bed, his own flattering estimate of himself. Verses 6 to 10 open with no warning onto the largest scale available, heavens, clouds, mountains, the great deep, and the grammar changes with the view, from he to You. Verses 11 to 13 then ask for the first panel to be kept away from the speaker. The word for wickedness at {{4.2}} returns at {{5.0}} and once more in the closing verse at {{13.3}}, which is the clearest signal that the panels were built to be read as one poem rather than two.

The first word is the surprise. {{2.0}} is the standard prophetic term for an oracle, normally followed by the divine name; here the one delivering the oracle is transgression itself. The Masoretic text then reads {{2.4}}, my heart, which places that oracle inside the speaker rather than inside the wicked man, while many manuscripts and the ancient versions read his heart instead, and modern translations still split over it. {{9.4}}, Your delights, is built on the same three consonants as the name Eden, so the stream of verse 9 and the garden are one word doing two jobs. {{7.1}} uses the divine name as an intensifier, mountains of God meaning the greatest mountains, and the parallel line answers it with the great deep.

The adverb at {{13.0}}, there, has nothing in the psalm to point at. The wicked have not been placed anywhere, and the fall is reported as though the reader had just watched it happen. Readings divide over what to supply: some take there as the place of the scheming in verse 5, the bed itself becoming the site of the collapse; others read it as a scene set ahead of the speaker, the psalm jumping to a judgment it never otherwise describes. The Hebrew tense supports both, since the perfect is used for what is finished and for what is treated as certain. Either way the last word, {{13.7}}, to rise, keeps the claim modest: the wicked are not said to be destroyed, only to be unable to get back up.

Verse 10 is the line the psalm exists for, and the mystical reading takes it literally. With You is the source of life, and {{10.4}}, in Your light, is the only medium in which light can be seen at all. Perception of the divine is then not an achievement of the eye but something on loan from what is being perceived, which is the exact answer to the two failed pairs of eyes in the first panel, {{2.9}} and {{3.3}}, which could see everything except themselves. The wings of {{8.7}} belong to the same picture: shelter here is not a wall but a shadow, and a shadow requires a body to be present before there is anything to sit under.
